item.title: cloudflare/security-audit-skill
item.description:
A coding-agent skill for multi-phase security audits with independently verified, machine-readable findings

security-audit

A coding-agent skill that turns your agent into a security auditor. It orchestrates isolated agents through reconnaissance, coverage-led hunting, candidate validation, structured output, independent record verification, and target-neutral reporting.

This is the skill that seeded Cloudflare's vulnerability discovery harness, described in Build your own vulnerability harness. The harness grew into a multi-stage, fleet-wide system; this skill is the single-repo starting point it evolved from.

What it does

The skill runs a structured audit in six phases:

  1. Reconnaissance -- map architecture, trust boundaries, input surfaces, prior evidence, and deterministic coverage in architecture.md and coverage-ledger.json.
  2. Coverage-led hunting -- assign isolated hunters from ledger units, record their checks, and use coverage critics to find gaps.
  3. Candidate validation -- give every unique candidate to a fresh verifier that tries to disprove it.
  4. Structured output -- write confirmed, needs_validation, and rejected records to findings.json and validate them against report-schema.json.
  5. Independent record verification -- fresh agents verify final source claims. Material replacements receive another independent verifier.
  6. Target-neutral reporting -- derive REPORT.md, FINDINGS-DETAIL.md, and NEEDS-VALIDATION.md from the verified records and coverage ledger.

The parent runs validate-coverage-ledger.cjs after creating the ledger and after each later ledger update. It runs validate-findings.cjs in Phase 4 and again after every Phase 5 replacement.

The verdicts are distinct: confirmed has a complete source trace and bounded observed result, needs_validation has an exact unresolved fact and no severity, and rejected records a disproved candidate.

Multiple runs against the same repo are additive. The skill uses prior ledgers and findings to target gaps, revalidate changed source, and carry forward current-source evidence without treating stale or unresolved work as covered.

Files

File Purpose
SKILL.md Setup, core principles, platform terminology, workflow overview, and audit anti-patterns
RECONNAISSANCE.md Phase 1 reconnaissance prompts and synthesis instructions
HUNTING.md Phase 2 orchestration, hunting methodology, and validation rules
ATTACK-CLASSES.md Core, wildcard, and obvious-things attack prompts
MEMORY-SAFETY-AND-BINARY.md Memory-safety, binary, and kernel hunting classes for native targets
AI-AND-LLM.md Prompt-injection, agent/tool, and output-handling hunting classes for LLM-backed targets
WEB-PROTOCOL-AND-AUTH.md HTTP request-framing, cache, and authentication-protocol hunting classes for HTTP-protocol and auth targets
CLIENT-SIDE.md DOM-injection, messaging-trust, UI-redress, and prototype-pollution hunting classes for client-side/browser targets
SUPPLY-CHAIN-AND-RELEASE.md Dependency, CI, release, signing, update, plugin, and extension hunting classes
CLOUD-AND-DEPLOYMENT.md IAM, infrastructure-as-code, container, serverless, ingress, and runtime-configuration hunting classes
PROTOCOLS-RPC-AND-MESSAGING.md RPC, serialization, queue, broker, webhook, and streaming-protocol hunting classes
RESOURCE-EXHAUSTION-AND-AVAILABILITY.md Shared resource, quota, queue, worker, and operator-spend hunting classes
DATA-ISOLATION-AND-LIFECYCLE.md Tenant isolation, cache, search, export, backup, migration, deletion, and restore hunting classes
DESKTOP-MOBILE-AND-LOCAL-IPC.md Native app, deep-link, webview, exported-component, helper, daemon, and local-IPC hunting classes
VALIDATION-AND-REPORTING.md Phases 3–6 candidate validation, structured output, record verification, and reporting
report-schema.json JSON schema for all three findings.json verdicts
validate-findings.cjs Zero-dependency validator for findings.json in Phases 4 and 5
validate-findings.test.cjs Findings-validator tests and producer-compatible fixture checks
validate-coverage-ledger.cjs Zero-dependency validator for coverage-ledger.json in Phases 1–5
validate-coverage-ledger.test.cjs Coverage-ledger validator tests

Installation

Install the skill with the Skills CLI:

npx skills add https://github.com/cloudflare/security-audit-skill \
  --skill security-audit

Use --global for a user-level installation:

npx skills add https://github.com/cloudflare/security-audit-skill \
  --skill security-audit \
  --global

Run npx skills --help for agent-selection and non-interactive options.

Usage

Start your coding agent in (or pointed at) the codebase you want to audit, then ask it to do a security audit:

security audit this codebase

find security vulnerabilities in ./src

do a security review, output to ~/audits/my-project

The skill activates automatically when the request matches its trigger (security audit, find vulnerabilities, pen-test the code, etc.). A direct codebase audit or pen-test request uses full audit mode. Security questions and focused vulnerability work use guidance mode unless you request report artifacts. In full audit mode, an unspecified output directory defaults to ~/security-audit-skill/<repo-name>/run-<N>. The workflow writes inside the target repository only when you explicitly select a directory that version control ignores.

Requirements

  • A coding agent with a model that supports tool use and parallel sub-agents
  • Node.js for the zero-dependency findings and coverage-ledger validators
  • An OS-enforced sandbox for target-controlled builds, tests, processes, browsers, emulators, fuzzers, and fixtures. It must disable external networking, use a sanitized allowlisted environment, enforce resource limits, and allow writes only to assigned scratch paths. Without these controls, the workflow keeps the lead as needs_validation instead of executing target code.

Design principles

  • Only confirm established boundary failures. Keep a source-grounded blocked lead as needs_validation with its exact unresolved fact.
  • Adversarial validation. The agent that checks a finding is never the agent that found it.
  • Severity requires impact. Likelihood x impact, not deviation from a checklist.
  • Defense-in-depth gaps are not vulnerabilities. If Layer A prevents the attack, the absence of Layer B is a hardening note.
  • Multiple runs improve coverage. In our test runs, a single run found roughly half of the vulnerabilities that repeated runs found in total.

Contact

Questions, feedback, or comparing notes on AI-driven security tooling: security-ai-research@cloudflare.com

item.title: mksglu/context-mode
item.description:
Free, local plugin that keeps tool output out of your coding agent's context window. Sandbox and SQLite FTS5 search, 99% fewer bytes in context. Works with Claude Code, Codex, Pi, OpenCode, Gemini CLI, Copilot CLI and 4 more agents. Zero telemetry.

https://contextmode.ai

Context Mode

A free, local plugin for 10 coding agents. It keeps tool output out of your agent's context window and keeps all usage data on your machine. The plugin is free forever.

33K GitHub stars · 683K npm downloads (read 2026-11-01, stats.json) · on the Hacker News front page and GitHub Trending: charts and sources

The Context Mode plugin is free and local, with its source open on GitHub. Context Mode Gateway is a separate hosted service with its own account and subscription. It takes the same idea from tool output to the whole conversation: Gateway Recall keeps long sessions searchable, and Gateway Memory shares what your agents learn across sessions and tools. See how the Gateway works

Contents: Why · Adoption · Install · Try it · Use cases · Benchmarks · How it works · Tools · Security and privacy · Context Mode Gateway · License · Community

Why

A coding agent reads files, runs commands and fetches pages, and every result goes into its context window. The Context Mode plugin runs that work in a local sandbox, keeps the full output in a SQLite index on your machine, and gives the agent the part it asks for.

  • The plugin is free forever. Use it at home and at work, free of charge, under a source-available license.
  • Runs on your machine. The hooks, the sandbox and search run as local processes next to your agent.
  • The plugin keeps your data on your machine. Every index lives in ~/.context-mode: one context.db per project.
  • Zero telemetry. The plugin keeps all usage data on your machine. Security and privacy lists each network call it makes.
  • Works offline after install. Sandbox runs, file indexing and search use local SQLite and your own runtimes.
  • Thinking in Code. The agent writes a short script instead of reading the data, and only what the script prints reaches the context: see How it works, step 5.
  • Small replies. On the 36 bench rows with 10 KB or more of raw output, the plugin's median reply is 99.4% smaller than the raw output.

Adoption: stars and npm downloads

Open the interactive chart and point at a bar to read its value. Tabs there show days, weeks, months and years. Stars come from the GitHub GraphQL API (starredAt); npm downloads come from api.npmjs.org/downloads/range. The total up to 2026-10-29 is 683K npm downloads (stats.json keeps a daily copy). A daily job redraws both charts.

  • Hacker News. "MCP server that reduces Claude Code context consumption by 98%" reached the front page with 570+ points and 107 comments on 2026-02-28 (thread).
  • GitHub Trending. A bot that watches GitHub Trending logged the repo there on 14 days from 2026-04-24 to 2026-10-17 (uibm/trending-watcher).

Starred by engineers at these companies: each name is the company field of 2 or more stargazer profiles, read with the GitHub GraphQL API on 2026-11-01 (data).

The npm route works for every agent:

npm i -g context-mode
context-mode setup

Setup is also the repair. It shows a plan, saves your earlier config, then applies the plan; when a step ends early, it restores the saved config. To uninstall:

context-mode setup --remove
npm rm -g context-mode

Restart the agent, then run /ctx-doctor in it. Each check prints PASS or a fix command, and the Doctor guide explains each check.

How we tested the install

Every agent gets hooks, the MCP server and the plugin skills; the last line of each block above says how. Hooks reach each agent in one of three ways: in the plugin package (Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Qwen Code), in a hook file (Codex, Copilot CLI, Kiro, VS Code, ZCode), or in a plugin inside the agent (OpenCode, Pi). The Agents guide shows what each agent runs. We ran the real binary of each agent with the plugin hook: Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, Qwen Code, Pi, OpenCode, Copilot CLI and ZCode. Each run used a clean temp home and a local test model, on 2.0.0-next.15. For VS Code and Kiro, the check covers the hook setup: VS Code runs the hook command with the documented payload, and kiro-cli 2.35.2 loads all 6 hook entries. CI runs setup, doctor, a hook and an MCP handshake for all 10 agents from the packed package on Linux, macOS and Windows. Record: HOOKS-FIRE.md. Each agent uses its own install command, and ADR-0023 says why.

Your first task with the plugin, step by step: First session. Or paste a prompt from Try it right now.

Try it

Paste one of these prompts into your agent after the install. Each one ran once, live, in Claude Code 2.1.312, and its answer matched the source data (evidence and rerun steps). The headline numbers in Benchmarks use the median of 5 runs. Other agents do the same job with the same tools: ctx_execute, ctx_index and ctx_search. After a prompt, run the stats skill and read the report yourself (See the saving).

On https://react.dev/reference/react/useEffect, show me the example that connects to a chat server and cleans up, and list the rules for the dependency array.

The hook sends WebFetch to the sandbox, and the agent searches the page for the example and the rules. 601,984 B raw, 20,860 B reached the context, 96.5% saved (2026-11-02, 2.0.0-next.26, claude-haiku-5-5).

Fetch https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/photos. Which photo has the longest title (give its id and title), and how many photos have a title that contains the word "est"?

The agent runs code over 5,000 JSON records in the sandbox and gets back two answers. 1,039,898 B raw, 393 B reached the context, 99.96% saved (2026-11-02, 2.0.0-next.26, claude-haiku-5-5). The answer is two short facts, so this is the best case of the four.

Here is a Linux syslog sample: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/logpai/loghub/master/Linux/Linux_2k.log. How many authentication failures does it contain, and which 3 remote hosts caused the most?

The agent counts failures in a 1,999-line syslog in the sandbox. 216,485 B raw, 566 B reached the context, 99.7% saved (2026-11-02, 2.0.0-next.26, claude-haiku-5-5).

What are the top 10 stories on the Hacker News front page right now? Give title, points and domain for each.

The hook sends WebFetch to the sandbox, and the agent reads ten stories from the page. 35,087 B raw, 1,501 B reached the context, 95.7% saved (2026-11-02, 2.0.0-next.26, claude-haiku-5-5). The front page changes, so the raw size changes with each run.

Benchmarks

Longer sessions

Say you debug a slow test all afternoon. The agent reads files, runs the suite and fetches docs, and each result goes into the context window. When the window is full, the host compacts it, and from then on the agent sees a short summary plus your next message.

Context Mode keeps the full output of each large tool call in context.db on your machine and gives the agent a small reply. At compaction, a snapshot of at most 2,048 B keeps the session state. After the compaction, the agent calls ctx_resume to read that snapshot back and ctx_search to find any earlier output by keyword.

In the bench, a scripted session of 40 tool outputs and one compaction made a 442,893 B transcript, and the ctx_resume block that brought the agent back was 2,019 B (row e-long-session in the bench file; open the case). In the same bench, one large log of 666,796 B put 3,380 B into the context, and the full log stayed in the index for ctx_search (row d-synth-1m; open the case). How the snapshot picks what to keep: the Long sessions guide and ADR-0009.

Next, what happens inside one tool call, in How it works.

How it works

One tool call, in time order, from the install to a hook error.

  1. Install. Each agent's own install command adds the MCP server, the hooks and the skills ctx-doctor, ctx-stats and ctx-upgrade to that agent's config folder, for example ~/.codex/skills/<name>/SKILL.md. context-mode setup writes or repairs any part the native command leaves out (ADR-0023).

  2. Session start. The SessionStart hook opens the project database. When the session ran before, the agent gets one line that tells it to call ctx_resume (dispatch.ts).

  3. PreToolUse checks. Before a tool runs, the PreToolUse hook checks the call in a fixed order: the user's deny list, WebFetch, curl and wget, inline HTTP and build commands, then a full-file Read over OUTPUT_CAP (16,384 B) and one-file shell dumps such as cat or tail. A Read with a line range runs as usual (decide.ts).

  4. The exact call. When a check matches, the hook stops the call and its reply names the exact ctx_* call to use, for example ctx_execute with {"language":"shell","code":"<the command>","intent":"<what you need>"}. For WebFetch the reply names ctx_index, then ctx_search (read-deny.ts).

  5. The sandbox. This is the Thinking in Code step: the agent's script runs here, and only what it prints comes back. ctx_execute writes the script to a temp folder and spawns the runtime from an argument list in the project folder. The timeout is EXEC_TIMEOUT_MS (600,000 ms, default and maximum); on timeout it stops the whole process group (taskkill /F /T on Windows). The child gets your environment minus preload variables such as NODE_OPTIONS, and the agent gets what the script prints, at most OUTPUT_CAP (execute.ts). Thinking in Code. The agent sends a short script as a tool parameter, the script reads the data in the sandbox, and only what it prints goes into the context.   6. Indexing. The full output goes into the index in chunks of at most MAX_CHUNK_BYTES (4,096 B). A Markdown chunk stays inside one heading section, and a code block that fits stays whole. Each chunk goes into two SQLite FTS5 tables: a Porter-stemmed table for words and a trigram table for paths, names and parts of words (fts.ts).

    ctx_index on a copy of this repo's docs/how-it-works.md, one live MCP call to release-out/server.mjs of Context Mode 2.0.0-next.36 on 2026-11-03 (calls.json). The file is 11,577 B; the agent gets 64 B.

  7. Search. ctx_search ranks each table with BM25 and joins the two lists with Reciprocal Rank Fusion: a hit scores 1/(RRF_K + rank), with RRF_K = 60. Before it returns an empty list, it tries a spelling fix from the indexed words. Search covers this session, this worktree (the default) or the whole project, and each snippet is at most SNIPPET_MAX_BYTES (800 B) (search.ts).

    ctx_search on that index, in the same run, in a project that also holds an AGENTS.md. One search reads the index and every agent's memory files. The agent gets 1,268 B: one content hit and one memory hit, each with its source and heading. For memory shared across machines, agents and sessions, see Context Mode Gateway Memory.

    ⏺ context-mode - ctx_search (MCP)(queries: ["compaction state block"])
  ⎿  Query "compaction state block":
     how-it-works.md #14: ### Session continuity
     
     The hooks log each prompt, edit, command, tool error, i…e same rows always give the same bytes.
     memory AGENTS.md #0: # Agent rules
     … +10 lines (ctrl+o to expand)

  8. Run, then replace. On hosts that run the tool first, the PostToolUse hook checks the result. Output over REPLACE_TRIGGER_BYTES (4,096 B) goes into the index whole, and the agent gets the best-matching chunks and one ctx_search line for the rest (dispatch.ts).

  9. Journal and compaction. The hooks log each prompt, edit, command, tool error and decision in a journal. After a compaction the agent gets a state block of at most STATE_BUDGET (2,048 B), and each long line becomes a ctx_resume(seq) pointer to the full row; one ctx_resume reply is at most RESUME_CAP (2,048 B). On the next prompt, a prompt-match block brings back the journal rows that match it by BM25 (ADR-0009).

    ctx_resume with empty parameters returns the state block, in the same run: 209 B.

    ⏺ context-mode - ctx_resume (MCP)()
  ⎿  <context_mode_state session="mcp:85e67fa2-28ef-45eb-9d5b-a967129b74c0" upto="2">
     indexed how-it-works.md
     source s1: how-it-works.md (11536 B)
     more: ctx_search(queries:[], scope:"session")
     </context_mode_state>

  10. The database. Each project has one context.db under ~/.context-mode, in Node's built-in node:sqlite. The database runs in WAL mode and runs a PASSIVE checkpoint on close. A new database gets built under a temp name and moves into place in one atomic step, and the busy timeout is DB_TIMEOUT_MS (5,000 ms) (db.ts).

  11. A hook error. A hook always ends with exit 0. On any error it gives the host's allow reply and writes one log line to ~/.context-mode/hook-errors.log, so your agent keeps working. A spawned hook has HOOK_TIMEOUT_MS (5,000 ms) (fallback.ts).

Every number with its reason: How it works. The rules the hook follows: ADR-0008. Next, the Tools the agent calls.

Tools

Tool What it does
ctx_execute Runs code or a shell command in a sandbox; returns what it prints
ctx_batch Runs many commands, indexes the output, and searches it in one call
ctx_index Indexes a file, a text or a URL into the project database
ctx_search Searches the local index; returns the matching parts
ctx_resume Returns the plugin's local state block (at most 2,048 B), or one full row by seq
ctx_stats Shows how much output stayed out of context
ctx_doctor Checks the install; each check prints PASS or a fix command
ctx_upgrade Installs, upgrades or uninstalls; replaces old contextmode entries
ctx_purge Deletes indexed data by session, source or project

Three more real calls, from the same live run of Context Mode 2.0.0-next.36 on 2026-11-03 (calls.json).

ctx_stats: the agent gets 3,097 B, the first line is the summary.

⏺ context-mode - ctx_stats (MCP)()

     … +59 lines (ctrl+o to expand)

ctx_doctor after context-mode setup --agents claude-code: 862 B, one row per check.

⏺ context-mode - ctx_doctor (MCP)()

     Environment: darwin-arm64, Node v26.8.1, shell /bin/zsh
     | Check | Status | Detail | Fix |

     | D1 version | PASS | 2.0.0-next.36 (8facf27): ahead of next on npm (2.0.0-next.34) |  |
     | D2 node | PASS | ok |  |
     … +11 lines (ctrl+o to expand)

ctx_purge deletes one source: 66 B.

⏺ context-mode - ctx_purge (MCP)(source: "how-it-works.md")
  ⎿  ctx_purge: deleted 18 rows (scope: source). This cannot be undone.

Full reference: Tools.

Commands in the agent: /ctx-stats shows the ctx_stats result, /ctx-doctor runs ctx_doctor (send its report with a defect report), and /ctx-upgrade runs ctx_upgrade, then ctx_doctor.

Security and privacy

  • The plugin keeps all its data on your machine, one database per project in ~/.context-mode, and ctx_purge deletes it by session, source or project. Read the Security guide.
  • The plugin has zero telemetry: usage data, events and crash reports stay on your machine. It uses the network for four calls, each one started by you or your agent:
Call When File
Fetch of a URL, for ctx_index Your agent asks for a page. The fetch blocks private and link-local addresses, checks each address the host name points to, connects to the address it checked, and checks again at each redirect. fetch.ts
One read of the npm dist-tags, with git ls-remote of the release tags as the fallback You run context-mode doctor, to check for a new version doctor-env.ts
npm i -g context-mode, or gh issue create You run context-mode upgrade, or you press a key to send the debug report commands.ts
Your agent's own install command, npm or git You install or update Your agent
  • The guard test D-PRIVACY-NET-1 in tests/0008-enforcement.test.mjs scans the source for HTTP clients, sockets, DNS lookups, git network calls and gh or npm spawns. It flags each new call site, so this table stays true.
  • Doctor and the debug report remove secrets by their structure before they print.

Code from ctx_execute runs on your host as your user, with your files, your network and your environment except the preload variables, so keep your agent's own permission prompts on. Here "sandbox" means the output stays in the sandbox and out of the context. What the plugin stores, where, and how to delete it: Privacy.

Context Mode Gateway

The plugin works on tool output, on your machine, and it is complete on its own. Context Mode Gateway is a separate hosted service with its own account and subscription. It works on every request, across all your agents. Its 11 features, the full list: Context Saving, Recall, Memory, Skills, Search, Session resume, Active Context, Instructions, Protect, Prompt caching, Live and Analytics. Add the Gateway when you want savings on every request, memory across sessions and agents, or cost reports for a team. For one project on one machine, the plugin covers the job. The two work together: Gateway guide. Gateway Recall, Search and Session resume run on the Gateway server, across sessions and agents. The plugin's ctx_search and ctx_resume read the local context.db of one project. With the Gateway on, your requests pass through its server; the plugin keeps its own data on your machine.

Product Runs Scope Billing
Context Mode plugin On your machine One project, local context.db Free
Context Mode Gateway Hosted service All sessions and agents Subscription, separate from the plugin

Set up the Gateway with one command:

npx @context-mode/cli

npx @context-mode/cli signs you in to your Gateway account, which has its own subscription, and writes one config change per agent. Apps: Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Codex, Codex Desktop, T3 Code, OpenCode and Pi. The Gateway CLI needs Node 20.12 or later, from its npm engines field.

item.title: Leonxlnx/taste-skill
item.description:
Agent skills that give coding agents taste: art direction, reference images and a browser check instead of generic AI pages

https://tasteskill.dev

     

Sponsors

interfaces.dev · A design engineering magazine by Jakub Krehel
React Bits · animated React components for creative interfaces
IMG.LY · CreativeEditor SDK
Sent.dm · messaging APIs for SMS, WhatsApp, and RCS

Become a sponsor

Taste Skill (tasteskill 2.5.0) is an Agent Skill that makes coding agents build professional company websites at the figma.com and x.ai level instead of assembling a generic landing page. Every build uses plain copy, one design system, one section per screen, equal left and right edges, real photographs, real brand icons and real product UI, with product renders when a product has no photographs, quiet micro-interactions, and shader effects, creative moments and scroll scenes kept strictly for tech, gaming and software pages, all verified in a real browser by a checker that enforces the rules.

Pages built from a single brief in earlier v2 runs:

The photographs are real, found in open archives and credited by the skill (credits). Watch the launch film.

Install

npx skills add https://github.com/Leonxlnx/taste-skill --skill "design-taste-frontend"

That installs the skill with the npx skills CLI.

The skill runs its scripts with Node 22+ and an installed Chrome, Edge or Chromium (set CHROME_PATH if it is in a non-standard place). Optional: ffmpeg on the PATH, for WebP output and the phone crop of a hero photograph in photos.mjs. It installs nothing and needs no API keys. Bundled Wikimedia Commons photographs work offline; fetching additional photographs or icons uses network access.

Claude Code plugin

Run these inside Claude Code. The skill is namespaced under taste-skill:, so it does not collide with your other skills.

/plugin marketplace add Leonxlnx/taste-skill
/plugin install taste-skill@taste-skill

/plugin update upgrades it later.

Codex plugin 
codex plugin marketplace add Leonxlnx/taste-skill
codex plugin add taste-skill@taste-skill

Start a new Codex session afterwards so the skill is loaded.

From a clone, linked instead of copied

./install.sh symlinks the skill into Claude Code (--codex for Codex, --all-agents for both), so a git pull updates it in place. On Windows (Git Bash) it makes a real link, or a directory junction when symlinks are not allowed, and it reports an older copied folder instead of skipping it silently.

Already have the skill? Run the install command again; the install name did not change. Looking for one of the older skills? See Moved skills.

How 2.5 works

Use it by asking your agent to build or redesign a company site; the agent loads the skill, copies assets/ into the project, starts from assets/starter.html and runs the checker before it hands the page over. Every build starts by classifying the client's business (software, gaming, tech, product, service or place) and planning the page screen by screen before writing markup:

  1. Deal tokens and layout. scripts/start.mjs deals a palette and Google Fonts pairing for the page kind (library/palettes.json, library/type.json), and assets/layout/deal.mjs deals a hero layout (split, centred, product, photo, place, collage, editorial, word, film, statement or triptych).
  2. Start from one system. assets/starter.html, assets/system.css and assets/layout/layout.css enforce one section per screen at desktop (1440x900), equal left and right content edges, a fixed navigation bar and a single-screen closing footer (footer.closing).
  3. Show real product UI and real photographs. Software and tech pages populate lit feature cards (assets/ui/cards.css) with rewritten HTML UI fragments (assets/ui/) and node-and-line diagrams (assets/diagrams/), with real brand and interface SVGs resolved locally by scripts/icons.mjs. Place, shop, hospitality and non-technical product pages lead with curated photographs (scripts/photos.mjs, assets/photos/), typography and flat colour, crediting sources in one expandable footer line with no captions under images.
  4. Keep effects for tech and gaming pages. Shader grounds (scripts/effects.mjs), creative scroll or pointer moments (scripts/moments.mjs), scroll scenes (assets/scenes/) and procedural 3D prints (assets/objects/) are dealt only on software, tech and gaming pages within a four-context WebGL cap, with static fallbacks for phones and reduced motion. Cafes, hotels, shops, studios and services get zero WebGL or scroll effects.
  5. Check in a real browser over HTTP. scripts/consistency.mjs, assets/layout/check.mjs, scripts/perf.mjs and scripts/shoot.mjs render the built page in headless Chrome across 1440, 1024, 768 and 390, catching empty visuals, broken shaders, contrast drops, misaligned columns, section-height drift, placeholder text, invented street numbers and slow-network image gaps before the build ships.

Details of what changed from 2.1.x are in the changelog.

The tools

Everything is a plain Node 22+ script in the skill folder; none installs anything.

Tool What it does
scripts/start.mjs Deals a palette and a Google Fonts pairing for the page kind and prints the <head> links and :root tokens.
assets/layout/deal.mjs Deals one of eleven tested hero layouts; assets/layout/check.mjs checks it with long-headline stress tests.
scripts/photos.mjs Deals vetted photographs by trade, enforces image weight and writes the one footer credit line.
scripts/icons.mjs Resolves real brand and interface icons into local SVG files.
scripts/effects.mjs, scripts/moments.mjs Deal shader grounds and creative moments for tech, gaming and software pages.
scripts/consistency.mjs The checker: renders the page in headless Chrome over HTTP at 1440, 1024, 768 and 390 and prints PASS, WARN or FAIL per rule.
scripts/perf.mjs, scripts/shoot.mjs Page weight and speed, and full-page and per-section screenshots.

First run: node scripts/start.mjs deal --page software (kinds: software, gaming, tech, product, service, place). Check a built page with node scripts/consistency.mjs <url or file> --page <kind>.

Moved skills

This repo holds one skill, design-taste-frontend. The others moved to repos of their own and kept their install names:

Install name Where it lives now
high-end-visual-design, minimalist-ui, industrial-brutalist-ui, gpt-taste, stitch-design-taste, design-taste-frontend-v1, design-taste-frontend-v2-experimental Leonxlnx/taste-skill-classics
imagegen-frontend-web, imagegen-frontend-mobile, brandkit, image-to-code Leonxlnx/imagegen-skills
redesign-existing-projects Part of design-taste-frontend, which audits an existing page in a real browser before changing anything
full-output-enforcement Removed. For the same problem, see Leonxlnx/unlazy

Install a moved skill from its new repo under the same name:

npx skills add https://github.com/Leonxlnx/taste-skill-classics --skill "high-end-visual-design"

Common Questions

What does the skill need?
Node 22 or newer and Chrome, Edge or Chromium; ffmpeg is optional (WebP photographs and the phone crop of a hero photograph). It installs nothing and uses no API keys. Bundled Commons photographs are stored locally; network access is used only when downloading additional photographs, Google Fonts or brand icons.

Where do the pictures come from, and can I use them?
From the skill's vetted photograph library (assets/photos/photos.json, including bundled Wikimedia Commons WebP sets and Unsplash photographs) dealt by scripts/photos.mjs. Library frames are used for trade and material details (or marked explicitly as draft stand-ins when the client has no photographs yet), never passed off as the client's own room, staff or product, and credited in one expandable footer line (photos.mjs credits).

Does it work with React, Vue, Svelte, plain HTML?
Yes. You can ship directly from assets/starter.html and the modular CSS/JS kits, or port the same tokens, section geometry, UI fragments and browser checks into React, Next.js, Vue, Svelte, Astro or Tailwind.

When does a page get shaders or scroll effects?
Only on software, tech (technical hardware) and gaming pages, and always within a four-context WebGL budget with static phone and reduced-motion fallbacks. Places, shops, cafes, hotels, studios, services and everyday physical products stay calm: photographs, sharp typography and flat colour.

item.title: mrdoob/three.js
item.description:
JavaScript 3D Library.

https://threejs.org/

three.js

JavaScript 3D library

The aim of the project is to create an easy-to-use, lightweight, cross-browser, general-purpose 3D library. The current builds only include WebGL and WebGPU renderers but SVG and CSS3D renderers are also available as addons.

Examples — Docs — Manual — Wiki — Migrating — Questions — Forum — Discord

Usage

This code creates a scene, a camera, and a geometric cube, and it adds the cube to the scene. It then creates a WebGL renderer for the scene and camera, and it adds that viewport to the document.body element. Finally, it animates the cube within the scene for the camera.

import * as THREE from 'three';

const width = window.innerWidth, height = window.innerHeight;

// init

const camera = new THREE.PerspectiveCamera( 70, width / height, 0.01, 10 );
camera.position.z = 1;

const scene = new THREE.Scene();

const geometry = new THREE.BoxGeometry( 0.2, 0.2, 0.2 );
const material = new THREE.MeshNormalMaterial();

const mesh = new THREE.Mesh( geometry, material );
scene.add( mesh );

const renderer = new THREE.WebGLRenderer( { antialias: true } );
renderer.setSize( width, height );
renderer.setAnimationLoop( animate );
document.body.appendChild( renderer.domElement );

// animation

function animate( time ) {

	mesh.rotation.x = time / 2000;
	mesh.rotation.y = time / 1000;

	renderer.render( scene, camera );

}

If everything goes well, you should see this.

Cloning this repository

Cloning the repo with all its history results in a ~2 GB download. If you don't need the whole history you can use the depth parameter to significantly reduce download size.

git clone --depth=1 https://github.com/mrdoob/three.js.git

item.description:
The fastest browser for AI agents to run browser automation, built for sharing your logged-in browser state with your AI agents, like Codex or Claude Code, without disturbing you. Zero cost, zero config.

https://lite.ego.app

The fastest browser for AI agents to run web automation

English · 简体中文 · 日本語 · 한국어 · Português · Español · Français · Italiano · Русский

ego (lite) is a browser where you and your AI agents work in parallel. Your agents run their browser tasks in their own Spaces, isolated workspaces inside the same browser, while you keep browsing in yours, so no agent ever takes the browser away from you. And the automation itself finishes faster, on fewer tokens.

Existing tools like browser-use and agent-browser are a bridge to the browser, not a browser of their own: they need a separate one to drive, your browser data rarely carries over intact, the connection is unstable, and you and the agent end up fighting over control of the browser. ego lite is one browser designed from the start for the two of you to share. No extra setup, and the agent can always reach your real logins and tabs through ego-browser.

Demo

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/ffe7954b-58ee-411e-b35d-ec30c58a08bc

Quick Start

ego lite runs on macOS and Windows, and Linux is on the roadmap.

1. Install

Pick whichever fits your flow.

1.1 Download the app

Click to download, then open it to install. Either way, ego lite adds the ego-browser skill to every agent's skills directory on your machine.

1.2 Add the skill with npx

Install just the ego-browser skill:

npx skills add citrolabs/ego-lite

The first time your agent runs a browser task, it walks you through installing the ego lite app.

1.3 Let your agent set it up

Paste this into your agent:

Set up ego lite for me: https://github.com/citrolabs/ego-lite

Read `skills/ego-browser/references/install.md` and follow the steps to install ego lite.

On first launch, ego lite asks one question, whether to migrate your Chrome data. Say yes and your agent inherits your existing logins, cookies, extensions, and bookmarks.

2. Try your first task

In your agent CLI, type /ego-browser followed by a space, then describe what you want in plain language:

ego-browser follow @ego_agent on x.com for me

The agent picks up the ego-browser skill, opens the page in its own Space, reads a Snapshot (the page turned into structured text), acts on the page, and reports back, all while your own tabs stay untouched.

Your browsing data, cookies, and everything else the browser holds stay on your device. ego lite keeps its data collection deliberately narrow: simple product signals, like whether you've set ego lite as your default browser.

Highlights of ego lite

Feature What it does
Code-based, not CLI-based: faster runs on fewer tokens for complex tasks The capabilities ego lite exposes to the agent are wrapped as JavaScript functions the agent calls directly. The agent gets to do what it does best: write code, composing a multi-step task into a single output instead of getting stuck in a "call two commands, look at the result, call two more commands" loop. Compared to the conventional CLI approach, complex workflows finish far faster, with higher task success rates, far fewer tool calls per task, and a much lower cost per task.
A dedicated Space for every agent ego lite gives each agent its own fully isolated Space. You browse up front, your agent works in the background, and they don't get in each other's way. You can see which Space has an agent running at any moment, and take it over or stop it whenever you want.
Your agents multitask in Spaces, parallel workspaces inside the same browser Each Space gets its own AI agent or its own task, all running at the same time. Claude Code enriching 10 leads in 10 parallel Spaces. Codex scraping 5 competitor sites in 5 more. They don't collide or steal your tabs. Your mouse stays where you left it.
The strongest page Snapshot on the market Thanks to customization inside the browser engine, ego lite produces the highest-quality page snapshots, the view text-only models rely on to "see" and act on a webpage. It reliably handles tough cases like deeply nested iframes, exactly where other approaches consistently break down.
Any agent can drive it through ego-browser ego-browser is the connection layer between any agent CLI (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, or a custom one) and ego lite. It exposes the browser as a set of in-page JavaScript tools: snapshot, fill, click, wait, navigate, capture. The agent writes a JavaScript snippet calling those tools, and ego-browser runs it on the page in one pass.
Experience accumulation that makes your agent faster the more you use it (coming soon) Most of an agent's time on browser tasks goes to trial and error. ego lite's official Skill distills every successful action into reusable tools and workflows, so similar tasks down the line run up to 5x faster.

ego lite vs existing products

Most tools can automate a browser. The real questions are what browser the agent gets, whether you can keep working at the same time, and whether the tool is built for the agent you already use or a built-in one.

Feature ego lite Browser extensions
Claude/Codex in Chrome		 Built-in browsers
Claude/ChatGPT built-in browser		 Cloud browsers
Browserbase/Browser Use		 Browser CLIs
playwright-cli/Browser Harness		 AI browsers
Comet/Dia
Works with any AI agent ✓ — — ✓ ✓ —
Uses your browser logins ✓ ✓ — — — ✓
Fewer CAPTCHAs ✓ ✓ — — — ✓
Works across your whole computer ✓ — ✓ — ✓ —
Doesn't hijack your browser ✓ — ✓ ✓ — —
Parallel multitasking ✓ — — ✓ — —
Runs large scraping jobs ✓ — — ✓ ✓ —
Works as your daily browser ✓ ✓ — — — ✓
Free ✓ — — — ✓ —
Data stored locally ✓ ✓ ✓ — ✓ —
Reusable skills (coming soon) ✓ — — — — —

Benchmarks

item.title: DuarteSantos8/openGym
item.description:
Open-source gym & body-weight tracker, now in the App Store (iPhone + Apple Watch) and as an Android APK. Plan routines, log workouts, see which muscles are trained, import from Strong/Hevy/FitNotes. Self-host it or use it on the phone alone.

https://opengym.ch

Website · Live demo · Roadmap · Changelog

Why openGym

Most workout apps keep your data on their servers, push you towards a subscription, or vanish when the company does. openGym runs on your own box, keeps your data in a folder you control, and is yours to fork. It still behaves like a modern app: installable on the home screen, passkey sign-in, works offline, syncs between your phone and your laptop.

No account on someone else's server, no subscription, no ads, no telemetry. One docker compose up and it's running.

The in-browser demo is the real app with example data, if you want to try it before installing anything.

Features

Planning

  • A routine per weekday over a library of over 5,600 exercises with animated demos, searchable and browsable by muscle on a body map. Filter by the equipment you own.
  • Four starter plans (Push/Pull/Legs, Upper/Lower, Full Body, 5×5) that load as ordinary, editable routines.
  • Every session on the Plan page and today's on Home carries a tiny body map with the muscles it works lit up, so you know Leg Day is legs before you open it.
  • Move a session to another day without touching the weekly plan. The week starts on Monday or Sunday, your choice.
  • Or skip the weekdays altogether: a rotation (A, B, C, A, ...) where the next session is simply the next one you haven't done, however the week went.
  • Supersets, warm-up sets, drop sets and rest-pause, timed exercises (planks, hangs, carries), cardio by time and speed, rest time per exercise, planned deloads.
  • Your own exercises, with your own photo, GIF or short video. Location data is stripped on the device before upload.

Training

  • Guided sessions: today's workout starts itself, weights are pre-filled from last time, a rest timer runs between sets, PRs are detected as you go. On a rest day it tells you when the next session is.
  • A quiet workout screen: one menu per exercise, the set number as the set's own menu, card or list view. Switches in Settings bring the old button rows back if you liked them.
  • Optional effort column as RIR or RPE, colour-coded, with a plain-language line per level.
  • Plate math for barbell, EZ bar, trap bar and Smith machine, worked out from the plates you own. Train in more than one place? Each gym keeps its own plates, dumbbells, bars and machine stacks, and the phone can switch to the gym you just walked into.
  • Bodyweight exercises know they carry no load: log reps, add a dip belt if you use one.
  • Per-side reps for lunges and single-arm work, the screen stays awake while you train, and a rest-timer alert can flash the screen for loud gyms.
  • Swipe a set left to delete it (with Undo) or right to copy it. Pyramid sets with their own reps and rest per set, and a scroll wheel for any rest time up to 15 minutes, or no timer at all.
  • Machine taken? A planned backup exercise swaps in with one tap and keeps the slot's sets and reps. Machines can carry their real weight stack, odd steps included, and progression sticks to it.
  • The session's volume runs live at the end of the progress bar.

Progress

  • Progression rules per routine or per exercise: linear, Greyskull LP, double progression through a visible rep range, triple progression (reps, then sets, then load), or adding time. Each target explains why it is that number; missed reps never add load, stalls trigger a deload.
  • Estimated 1RM per exercise with its own curve, Structural Balance ratios (Poliquin, Thibaudeau, ATG), a year-long activity heatmap.
  • A muscle map in three modes: where your volume went, what is still recovering, and what has gone untrained.
  • Body-weight chart against a goal line, with your weekly rate and an optional lose, gain or hold range, and progress photos on a timeline with a before/after slider.
  • Lifts as a percentage of body weight, and a running total of everything you've ever lifted.
  • Edit any saved workout after the fact, log one you did on paper, or move it to the right date. Records are re-read from the corrected history.

Accounts and data

  • Passkeys (Face ID, Touch ID, fingerprint) with per-profile data synced across devices. Password sign-in can be switched on per instance; new devices pair with a one-time code or QR.
  • Two devices editing at once merge field by field instead of overwriting each other (see sync).
  • Import from FitNotes, Strong, Hevy (CSV or API key) and Apple Health weight exports. Export everything as one JSON file, or your workouts and body data as a spreadsheet (CSV).
  • Share a plan as a small file or print it as a PDF.
  • Optional admin dashboard with invite-only signup and an activity log.
  • 20 languages, including right-to-left Arabic and Traditional Chinese. Exercise names and instructions are translated for most of them.

On the phone and the wrist

  • Apps for iPhone, iPad and Android that work on their own (no server, no account) or connected to yours. Rest timer in the notification shade, reminders, and Health Connect or Apple Health in both directions: workouts go out, weigh-ins and heart rate per set come back in.
  • A gym reminder, off by default: walk into one of your gyms and the phone nudges you to hit Start. Once a day at most, never after you trained, and your gyms stay on the phone.
  • An Apple Watch app: tick off sets with the Digital Crown, RPE or RIR right on the wrist, a full-screen rest countdown, heart rate per set, a Lock button against stray crown presses, and complications. No watch? AirPods Pro 3 do the heart rate on iOS 26.
  • Widgets and a Live Activity on the iPhone: log a set, skip the rest or jump to the next exercise from the Lock Screen without opening the app.

Only what you use

  • Modules: switch whole parts of the app on and off in Settings → Modules, from "Just training" to "Everything". Body, Health, Motivation, the Coach, seasonal themes and more each disappear completely while they're off, and nothing is deleted.

Optional extras, off by default

  • An AI coach that drafts a week of routines and later suggests changes based on what you logged, and answers questions about your training. You approve every change. It runs on your server, or on the phone alone, with your own provider key (Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint, Ollama included).
  • An MCP server so an assistant like Claude Desktop can answer questions about your training history, and log a workout you describe to it. Local; not part of the Docker build.
  • Integrations in one place: Apple Health, Health Connect (Garmin, Fitbit, Withings and friends come in through them), imports, and signed webhooks to Home Assistant, n8n or ntfy when you finish a workout, set a record or weigh in.

The full list of what changed release by release is in the changelog.

Quick start

You need Docker with Compose.

git clone https://github.com/DuarteSantos8/openGym
cd openGym
cp .env.example .env
docker compose pull      # prebuilt images, amd64 + arm64 (skip this to build from source)
docker compose up -d

Open http://localhost:8080, tap Create profile, and you're in. The exercise animations are part of the image, so there's nothing else to download.

To reach it from your phone with passkeys you need HTTPS on a domain; that's a two-line change in .env. The self-hosting guide walks through Cloudflare Tunnel, Caddy, Traefik and nginx, and there are separate guides for HTTPS on a LAN, a Mac with Tailscale and Kubernetes.

Note

Images are published from the same tag to ghcr.io/duartesantos8/opengym-{api,web} (what docker-compose.yml pulls) and registry.gitlab.com/duartesantos8/opengym/{api,web}. Swap the image: lines if you prefer GitLab's registry, or run docker compose up -d --build to build locally. Either way you don't need Node on the host.

Configuration reference (all through .env)
Variable What it does Default
RP_ID Hostname passkeys are bound to localhost
ORIGIN Full URL the app is served from http://localhost:8080
WEB_PORT Host port for the web UI 8080
NGINX_PORT Port the web container listens on inside the container 80
BACKEND Name of the API service that /api is proxied to api
PORT Port the API listens on; the web container proxies to the same value 3000
RP_NAME Name shown in the passkey prompt openGym
SESSION_DAYS How long a sign-in lasts, in days 90
ADMIN_UIDS User ids that get the admin dashboard, comma-separated (none)
FIRST_USER_ADMIN 1: the first profile created on an empty instance becomes its admin (off)
INVITE_ONLY Require an invite code to create a profile (off)
ALLOW_GUEST Offer "Continue without account"; 0 requires a profile (on)
PASSWORD_LOGIN Offer name-and-password sign-in next to passkeys (off)
TRUST_PROXY Let the sign-in throttle read the client address from proxy headers 1 in docker-compose.yml
AUDIT_LOG Record sign-ins and admin actions; 0 records nothing (on)
AUDIT_MAX Events kept in the activity log; 0 for no limit 5000
AUDIT_DAYS Days kept in the activity log; 0 keeps until AUDIT_MAX 90
AUDIT_IP Record the caller's address: off, net (network only) or full off
ALLOWED_PRIVATE_IPS Private addresses push endpoints may resolve to (FakeDNS, split-horizon DNS): comma-separated IPs, a-b ranges or CIDR blocks (none)
INTEGRATIONS Server integrations to offer, comma-separated: webhook (integrations) (none)
INTEGRATIONS_ALLOW_LAN 1: webhooks may reach your home network (Home Assistant), http included; never loopback (off)
VAPID_SUBJECT Contact URL sent with push notifications your ORIGIN
API_TARGET API image to build: default, or coach with the Claude Agent SDK and Codex CLI default
COACH_DISABLED 1 forces the AI coach off instance-wide (unset)

Push-notification keys are generated on first run into ./data/vapid.json. DATA_DIR is pinned to /data inside the container and mapped to ./data on the host; change the volume, not the variable. The self-hosting guide covers every option in detail.

Phone app

The same codebase builds the phone apps with Capacitor. Use them on their own (everything stays on the phone, no account) or connect them to your server and sync.

Get it
iPhone and iPad, with the Apple Watch app The App Store, in every App Store country
Android The signed APK from the latest release or opengym.ch, in three sizes: Standard (openGym-X.Y.Z.apk, animations at 180 px, about 315 MB), Plus (openGym-Plus-X.Y.Z.apk, 240 px, about 424 MB) and HD (openGym-HD-X.Y.Z.apk, 360 px, about 760 MB). It updates itself and stays the kind you picked
Google Play In closed testing: Google wants 12 testers for 14 days before it lets everyone in. Join the tester group, then opt in. It installs right over the APK and keeps your data
Wear OS watch (beta) Rides along with the Google Play test: once Google's watch review is done, "openGym Beta" shows up in the Play Store on your Galaxy Watch, Pixel Watch and friends. Details: docs/WEAR_OS.md

Every APK sits next to its .sha256. The APK and the Play app share one signing key, so you can switch between them (or between Standard, Plus and HD) without losing data. Details, building it yourself and connecting to your server: docs/MOBILE.md.

How it works

  • frontend/ is React 19 and Vite (React Router, Zustand), built to static files inside Docker.
  • api/ is plain node:http with three dependencies: @simplewebauthn/server for passkeys, web-push for notifications and undici for the AI coach's provider calls. Everything is stored as JSON under ./data.
  • web/ builds the frontend and serves it with nginx, proxying /api so the whole app sits on one origin, which passkeys require.

The architecture overview has the longer version, with diagrams of the frontend, sync, the exercise media and the watch.

The training logic (progression rules, 1RM, how a logged session is read back) lives in pure functions under frontend/src/lib/ with tests beside them. The HTTP API is documented as an OpenAPI spec in api/openapi.yaml, browsable at opengym.ch/api.html.

How sync works

Each profile's data is one document with a server revision. A device sends the revision it last saw along with its changes; if another device wrote in between, the server refuses and returns the current document so the device can merge and retry. Every change carries its own stamp, down to a single setting or routine field, so the merge keeps the newest edit of each one and a deletion stays deleted.

Nothing that hasn't reached the server is discarded on disconnect or sign-out, and the app shows a banner whenever it's working offline.

Your data

Everything lives in ./data on your host:

File Contents
db.json Profiles and public passkey data
db.json.bak A copy of the last good db.json, used if the main file can't be read
state-<user>.json Each user's plan, workouts, body weight and settings
audit.log Admin activity log (no IP addresses unless you turn that on)
secret Session-cookie signing key

Back up ./data and you've backed up everything. Passkey private keys never reach the server; they stay in your phone's secure hardware or your password manager.

Documentation

The documentation index sorts every guide by who it's for. The most used ones:

I want to Read
Get a quick answer FAQ
Set up my own instance Self-hosting
Use the Android or iPhone app Phone app
Bring my history from another app Importing data
Turn on the AI coach AI coach
Contribute code Contributing
Report a security problem Security

Roadmap

A release roughly every one to two weeks, each one whatever has passed testing by then. The full plan is in ROADMAP.md, and the issues sit in the GitHub milestones.

Release When Theme
v1.4.0 released Oct 2026 A new exercise database with 5,632 exercises, plus two rounds of community work
v1.4.1 released Oct 2026 Bug fixes for v1.4.0
v1.4.2 released Oct 2026 The App Store, the Apple Watch, widgets, three APK sizes
v1.4.3 released Oct 2026 The Halloween and community release: gym reminder, health data read back, watch upgrades, CSV export
v1.4.4 released Nov 2026 Programmes, a fresh look, Modules, a tour with tutorials, AirPods heart rate, kg or lb per exercise, the Google Play closed test and a Wear OS beta
v1.4.5 Nov 2026 Google Play for everyone, F-Droid, Settings → Integrations (Strava, webhooks, calendar, Nextcloud), timed holds that start themselves
v1.4.6 Dec 2026 Wear OS out of beta, deeper Health Connect, body composition
v1.4.7 Dec 2026 The progression engine by @giulioleuci, circuits, AMRAP and EMOM
later dates are guesses Search and catalogue, accounts, a trainer role, skins, Garmin, database storage

Community

  • Discord for release announcements, self-hosting help and quick back-and-forth. Usually the fastest way to get an answer.
  • Discussions for questions and ideas you want the next person to find by searching.
  • Issues for reproducible bugs and agreed-on work. Login trouble is almost always an RP_ID/ORIGIN mismatch; the self-hosting guide covers it.
  • Pull requests are welcome; start with CONTRIBUTING.md.

Where the code lives

GitHub is the home of the project. gitlab.com/DuarteSantos8/opengym is a mirror, updated by a GitHub Actions workflow on every push to main and every release tag. It exists because its CI builds the multi-arch images and the SBOMs for its registry (the APKs are built and signed on the release machine and attached to the GitHub release). Nothing is merged there by hand. In the changelog, !NN refers to a GitLab merge request from the weeks in August and September 2026 when the project lived there.

How openGym is built

People have asked about this, so plainly: openGym is developed with Claude Code, Anthropic's coding agent. A large share of the code, tests and documentation is drafted in Claude Code sessions, and the repository carries a CLAUDE.md with the project context those sessions start from.

What that does and doesn't mean:

  • A person decides and ships. What goes in, what gets reviewed and merged, and every release are the maintainer's call. Changes are tested on a staging instance and on real phones before they are tagged.
  • Tests hold the logic in place. The training logic is covered by unit tests, and pull requests run the frontend, API and MCP suites in CI. That is the guard against plausible-looking code that is wrong, whoever or whatever wrote it.
  • The app itself doesn't need an LLM. Nothing in a default install calls an AI service. The AI coach and the MCP server are opt-in, and the coach only talks to the provider you configure, with your own key.

Community pull requests are written by their authors, with whatever tools they like, and reviewed the same way.

Support

openGym is free and stays free: AGPL, no paid tier, nothing held back for sponsors. If it replaced a paid tracker for you and you'd like to chip in, there's Buy Me a Coffee, Ko-fi and GitHub Sponsors (the app has the same three under Settings → About & updates, and on the iPhone a shortcut to leaving an App Store review). A star, a bug report or a pull request helps just as much.

GitHub Sponsors

License

openGym's own code is licensed under the GNU AGPL v3.0. You can self-host, use, modify and share it; if you run a modified version as a network service, you have to offer that version's source under the same license.

Important

The exercise media is not covered by that license. The stills and animations are © Aliaksandr Makatserchyk, Gym visual, licensed for use in openGym only: 180 px in this repository and on self-hosted servers, larger only inside the app packages. A non-commercial fork may keep them unmodified with the notice; anything else needs your own licence from gymvisual.com. The exercise text in catalogue/ is openGym's and open to contributions.

Contributing: pull requests are signed off once with the Contributor License Agreement: you keep the copyright in your work, openGym may use and relicense it (so the app can stay in the App Store and Google Play long term), and every version released under the AGPL stays AGPL.

Full third-party notices, including the body-diagram geometry, are in NOTICE.md.

item.title: withmarbleapp/os-taxonomy
item.description:
Marble Skill Taxonomy

An open, structured taxonomy of what children learn across the primary/elementary years — decomposed into fine-grained "micro-topics", wired into a prerequisite graph, and aligned to national curriculum standards. Produced by Marble.

Version: v1 · Topics: 1,861 · Prerequisite edges: 4,003 · Subjects: 9

See it

Every dot is a micro-topic, colored by subject; height is age; each thread is a prerequisite (full-quality video). Explore it interactively at withmarble.com/curriculum — tap any concept to trace everything a learner must master before it.

What this is

Most curriculum data is either a flat list of standards or locked inside a product. This dataset is a connected graph of learning:

  • 1,861 micro-topics — a single, teachable idea (e.g. "Building sentences", "Apparent brightness of stars"), each with a plain-language description, mastery evidence criteria, a type (conceptual / procedural / representational / language / meta), a subject + domain, and an approximate age range.
  • 4,003 prerequisite dependencies — a directed acyclic graph: "topic X depends on prerequisite Y", each edge tagged hard/soft and carrying a one-line reason.
  • Curriculum alignment — each micro-topic links to the standards it was distilled from (NGSS, Common Core, the UK National Curriculum, and more).
  • Teaching research — 1,049 records. Coverage is partial; 812 topics have no research in this release.
  • Domain clusters — 176 parent-friendly one-paragraph summaries per (subject, domain, age band).

Subjects

Subject Topics
Computing 52
English 339
Geography 22
History 109
Learning to Learn 18
Life Skills 46
Mathematics 581
Personal & Social Development 118
Science 576

Files

All data lives in data/ as UTF-8 JSON. See schema/ for JSON Schemas and manifest.json for counts + SHA-256 checksums.

File What it holds
data/topics.json The micro-topics (graph nodes).
data/dependencies.json Prerequisite edges (topicId depends on prerequisiteId).
data/curriculum-standards.json The source curriculum standards, grouped by curriculum.
data/clusters.json Parent-friendly domain summaries.
data/teaching-research.json Teaching research joined by topicId, with explicit coverage and publication notes (~24 MB).
data/archived-teaching-research.json Historical guidance for merged or refocused topics, with original records and current topic associations.
data/manifest.json Counts, per-subject breakdown, per-file checksums.
data/curriculum-alignments.json Scoped framework, jurisdiction and global age contexts; source for flat compatibility fields.

The catalogue contains 17 sources / 7,743 expectations. It includes 620 Australian Curriculum v9 content descriptions and 3,862 Ontario expectations from nine elementary documents. Ontario is exported as codes and official source links only; ingestion of source expectations is separate from authoring topic coverage. Ontario Grades 1–7 Mathematics have received focused taxonomy authoring passes. The Grade 2 report distinguishes reused claims, extracted elementary claims and the concurrency gap; mappings do not certify learner mastery of every linked topic. The Grade 3 report records reuse of 114 existing topics, the congruence extension and prerequisite repairs; no topics were added. The Grade 4 report records reuse of 126 existing topics, two missing skills, two focused extractions and prerequisite repairs. The Grade 5 report records reuse of 145 existing topics, one missing mathematical representation, one financial/civic concept and one focused extraction. The Grade 6 report records reuse of 173 existing topics and five additions: two procedures, one focused extraction and two financial-content claims. The Grade 7 report records reuse of 171 existing topics and two spatial additions; the square-root proposal was withdrawn.

Ontario Grade 5 Language adds 306 links across 161 existing topics, with no new topics. The Grade 5 Language report and code-by-code mapping record whole-topic reuse, prerequisite repairs, and the four remaining resource/performance conditions. Coverage links do not certify learner mastery.

Ontario Grade 6 Language adds 313 links across 168 topics, including three new claims and a suffix-evidence correction. The Grade 6 Language report and code-by-code mapping record 55 Full / 4 Partial specific expectations, with resource and performance conditions retained. This Language pass stops at primary Grade 6 (ages 11–12).

The Australian cleanup reviewed all 314 additions and 14 later edited IDs, consolidated repeated skills and redistributed bundled requirements. All 593 selected expectation codes remain linked. Those links do not certify whole-standard coverage: 572 previous Full claims have not been independently recertified. The 27 PE/movement descriptions remain excluded. Read the cleanup report and current area-by-area mapping counts.

See PROVENANCE.md for sources and attribution.

Adding curricula

The public alignment contract now has a reviewed baseline of 3,733 contexts. Edit data/curriculum-alignments.json for associations and their ages; keep topic claims in data/topics.json. The version 2 scope model preserves global guidance, international frameworks and separate jurisdiction age intervals on one topic; version 1 remains supported by the codec.

Run npm run alignments:generate, npm run validate, npm run alignments:generated-check and npm test, then submit the actual data change in a normal PR. Generation refreshes flat topic standards/ages, the research file's topic checksum binding and manifest checksums/counts. It uses only public local files and preserves original timestamps; no private account is needed. Authored research and its coverage must already be valid; this bounded command does not author research or repair unrelated artifacts.

The authoring and publication design describes downstream application deployment. This public baseline does not apply changes to a live DB, migrate agent tools or activate the future publisher.

Curricula map onto one shared taxonomy. Keep subjects and domains consistent across countries; a curriculum's learning-area labels do not create separate subject trees.

  • Reuse a topic when it assesses the same concept or operation. Add local examples without changing what mastery means.
  • Review affected assessment guidance and learner estimates before changing a mastery claim. Assess independent procedures separately; topics do not track multiple difficulty levels.
  • Record whole-expectation, component and prerequisite contributions explicitly. A topic–code link alone does not establish Full coverage.
  • Reuse existing domains before adding a distinct new domain. Keep names consistent and avoid parallel country-specific domain trees.
  • Keep each topic focused on a teachable concept or skill. A standard can link to several topics; its bundled requirements need not become one topic.
  • Add country-specific topics where the knowledge genuinely differs, such as a country's history or constitutional arrangements. Use shared topics for common concepts and skills, with local examples where useful.

A topic

{
  "id": "mt_N8CpN1EJrP",
  "type": "CONCEPTUAL",
  "subject": "English",
  "domain": "Grammar & Punctuation",
  "name": "Building sentences",
  "description": "Understand that words combine to make sentences — a sentence expresses a complete thought…",
  "ageRangeStart": 4,
  "ageRangeEnd": 6,
  "centrality": 0.257,
  "evidence": [
    "Distinguish between complete sentences and fragments",
    "Compose a complete sentence with a subject and verb"
  ],
  "assessmentPrompt": "If {{name}} says something like \"The dog\", can they tell you that's not a complete sentence…?",
  "standards": ["ccss-ela:L.K.1f", "uk-nc-2013:Eng.App2.Y1.Sent.1"]
}
  • id — stable identifier (mt_…), referenced by dependencies and by neighbours.
  • standards — keys into curriculum-standards.json ("<curriculum-slug>:<code>").
  • assessmentPrompt — a natural-language check for the idea. Contains a {{name}} placeholder (the child's name); substitute or strip before display.

A dependency

{ "topicId": "mt__00ZSLnB7p", "prerequisiteId": "mt_VBl1T1sFCM", "strength": "hard",
  "reason": "Must understand vibrations make sound before finding volume patterns" }

topicId depends on prerequisiteId. Reverse the edge to get "unlocks".

Teaching research

data/teaching-research.json adds how a topic might be taught to the graph of what children learn. It contains 1,049 active topic records. coverage.missingTopicIds and per-subject counts make the 809 topics without research explicit; absence is not a judgement about whether a topic can be taught.

archived-teaching-research.json preserves two historical records excluded from active coverage after a topic merge and a change in learning scope. Each entry includes the original topic and research record, its archive reason, and related current topic IDs. The archive also records the assessment prerequisite reference redirected after the merge.

The active teaching-research.json file has schemaVersion: 1 and taxonomy version: "v1". Each records[] entry joins topics.json through topicId and contains:

Field Meaning
pedagogy Original teaching summary, practices, representations and misconceptions.
learn Portable learning guidance (schemaVersion: 2): a summary, activities, educational constraints and review notes.
learn.activities[] Learner actions, intended insight, feedback, rationale and supporting source claims. No product artifact types or fit rankings.
assess Original diagnostic/task, response levels, error patterns and next teaching moves; nullable in the public interface.
sources Claim, named source, optional URL and the original author's verification flag.
confidence Original authoring confidence; not an independent quality score.
provenance Original authoring model and source record timestamps. The update timestamp also reflects the learning-guidance rewrite.
publicationNotes Paths and curriculum codes for text omitted under the codes-only publication policy.

sourceClaims exactly match sources[].claim after publication transformations. A source may support a general principle or curriculum alignment; this does not mean the proposed activity was tested. Some activities have no directly linked source claim.

These records were agent-authored. The learning guidance was rewritten for portability, checked by a separate factual critic, and sampled by a second agent. Most original pedagogy and assessment were retained and may contain claims that the updated guidance qualifies; chart-specific alignment repairs after #30 are recorded in the affected learning-guidance review notes; read the constraints and review notes alongside them. Sources were not re-fetched or re-verified for the initial publication; later nutrition-guide checks are recorded in the affected review notes. Historical verified: true and confidence: "high" are not new evidence ratings. Activities are research-informed proposals, not empirically validated interventions.

Nutrition terminology corrections in #63 update the existing Animal Nutrition, Balanced Diet & Food Groups, and Nutrients in a Healthy Diet guidance, activities and assessment to distinguish nutrients from food groups. Balanced-plate activities use food groups in a local guide; the records retain their identities. See the review note.

Some original research quoted restricted curriculum standards. Matched passages are replaced with inline curriculum references, including inside citation claims; all transformed paths are listed in publicationNotes. This is a conservative mechanical omission pass, not comprehensive rights clearance. Consult the linked upstream sources for their wording and terms. See PROVENANCE.md.

After the chart split in #30, mt_bESTSBB0wK covers pie charts, mt_H6LlpWgEYS covers earlier line-graph problem-solving, and mt_HlNSurPVDp has a separate construction-and-interpretation record. The new record adapts existing graph research; it is not a fresh literature review, and all reused source-verification flags are false. Its assessment requires a complete constructed graph. The later grouped-charts assessment routes graph-choice errors to data presentation and sector-angle errors to pie charts.

The file is bound to the exact topics.json bytes through topicFileSha256. Regenerate the research projection when the canonical topic file changes, even when topic IDs remain stable.

Using it

Pure data — no runtime, no dependencies. Load the JSON and go.

import topics from './data/topics.json' with { type: 'json' };
import deps from './data/dependencies.json' with { type: 'json' };

const byId = new Map(topics.topics.map(t => [t.id, t]));
const prereqs = deps.dependencies
  .filter(d => d.topicId === 'mt_N8CpN1EJrP')
  .map(d => byId.get(d.prerequisiteId).name);

Join teaching guidance to a topic:

import research from './data/teaching-research.json' with { type: 'json' };

const guidanceByTopic = new Map(research.records.map(r => [r.topicId, r]));
const guidance = guidanceByTopic.get('mt_N8CpN1EJrP'); // undefined: English is not covered yet
const activities = guidance?.learn.activities ?? [];

Validate structure, research coverage, evidence links and checksums:

node scripts/validate.mjs
node --test scripts/teaching-research.test.mjs

Marble Builder

The marble-builder agent skill helps turn a child's age and a user-confirmed goal into a standalone HTML learning experience that works offline by default. It uses topic prerequisites and available teaching research, develops a targeted research brief when needed, and agrees a concept with you before building. Experiences use visual interactions, scaffolding, UI-assessed transfer tasks and optional extensions. Spatial topics use Three.js with direct scene manipulation and a crafted cel-shaded look with flat colors and black outlines. Visual simulations must meet a beauty, craft and polish bar as well as work correctly. The public skill includes Marble-derived UI tokens, tactile controls refined in Moon Visit and Sky Colour Explorer, and the openly licensed Baloo 2 font, with one title and one instruction visible at a time: a small top-left title and a large, prominent instruction or explanation, plus concise button labels paired with icons. Water Lab is the visual quality reference. The agent renders, inspects and iterates in the browser rather than stopping at the first working HTML file.

The skill includes five runnable examples with readable source, key-state screenshots and design notes: Moon Visit, Sky Colour Explorer, Hidden Cubes, Bee Builder and Otter Forest. The notes explain what to borrow and where each prototype has limits or exceptions.

Optional connected LLM mode requires explicit author approval and a learning goal whose open-ended reasoning or text production cannot be adequately supported locally. That mode requires internet and a separate account connection; ChatGPT plan usage is a preview option for eligible local/open-source integrations.

In Codex, open this repository and invoke $marble-builder, for example:

Use $marble-builder to help my 8-year-old understand why equivalent fractions represent the same quantity.

Other agents can follow the linked SKILL.md directly. No Marble account or hosting is required. New reusable teaching research can optionally be proposed as a separate PR, with no child-specific information included.

License

This dataset is multi-licensed — read this before you use or redistribute it.

Layer License
The database — the collection, structure, IDs, topic↔topic and topic↔standard relationships ODbL 1.0 — free for research and commercial use, attribution required, share-alike (derivative databases must stay open under ODbL).
The textual content Marble authored — topic description/name/evidence/assessmentPrompt, dependency reasons, cluster summarys, original teaching-research prose CC BY-SA 4.0 — same spirit: attribution + share-alike.
Marble-authored learning examples — application source, original artwork, captures and design notes CC BY-SA 4.0. Bundled Three.js and Baloo 2 retain their separate MIT and OFL licenses and notices.
curriculum-standards.json — extracted from third-party frameworks Not Marble's to relicense. Each source is under its own upstream license — see PROVENANCE.md.

Why share-alike + still commercial-friendly: ODbL distinguishes a derivative database (extend/modify the taxonomy → must stay open) from a produced work (use it inside a product, model, or app → stays yours). So you can build a commercial product on this without open-sourcing your product; you only owe back improvements to the taxonomy itself.

Attribution

Any use must credit:

Marble Skill Taxonomy (v1) · © Generative Spark, Inc. (Marble) · https://withmarble.com · licensed under ODbL 1.0 (database) and CC BY-SA 4.0 (content).

Plus the upstream notices in PROVENANCE.md for any curriculum standards you use. See CITATION.cff for a formal citation.

What's not here

Deliberately excluded from this release: semantic embeddings (derived, recomputable) and any per-child / user data (never published). See CHANGELOG.md.

Install ECC

Important

ECC 2.2 includes guided package setup for Claude Code, Codex, and Kimi Code. The universal package requires Node.js 18 or newer. Claude plugin setup also requires Git and Claude Code 2.1 or newer on PATH.

Recommended: universal guided setup

For Claude Code plugin setup, updates, scope changes, and hook-profile changes:

npx ecc-universal@2.2.3 setup

Windows first-time walkthrough

If you are new to command-line tools, use this copy-and-paste path:

  1. Install Node.js 18 or newer, Git, and Claude Code.

  2. Open PowerShell from the Windows Start menu.

  3. Confirm that each prerequisite is available:

    node --version
git --version
claude --version

  5. For a typical personal setup, choose Global user, choose Standard hooks, and confirm.

  6. Start a new Claude Code session and run /plugin list to verify that ecc@ecc is enabled.

Claude Code details

Alternatively, run Claude Code's native plugin commands inside Claude Code:

/plugin marketplace add https://github.com/affaan-m/ECC
/plugin install ecc@ecc

The native path installs ECC's skills, agents, commands, and plugin-managed hooks. If you choose it, stop there. Do not also run a full manual install into Claude Code.

Claude Code owns these built-in commands, including their errors when a marketplace, plugin, or conflicting scope already exists. ECC cannot intercept that parser. If either native command reports an existing install or scope conflict, use the 2.2 guided setup or resolve the conflicting Claude plugin scope before retrying; do not layer a manual install on top.

After ECC is installed, /ecc:configure-ecc is the namespaced in-Claude reconfiguration skill. It delegates to the same safe setup flow, but it is available only after the plugin is installed and cannot replace Claude Code's built-in /plugin command during a first install.

Claude Code plugins cannot distribute rules, so add only the rule packs you actually want:

git clone https://github.com/affaan-m/ECC.git
cd ECC
mkdir -p ~/.claude/rules/ecc
cp -R rules/common ~/.claude/rules/ecc/
cp -R rules/typescript ~/.claude/rules/ecc/  # replace with your stack

Start with rules/common plus one language or framework pack you actually use. If you install the plugin, do not run ./install.sh --profile full afterward.

Prefer settings.json? Add the marketplace declaratively

Add directly to your ~/.claude/settings.json:

{

        "repo": "affaan-m/ECC"
      }
    }
  },

    "ecc@ecc": true
